evaluated_by: Human researched draft using official and institutional sources
overall_summary: Uruguay is a relatively stable, institutionally strong Southern Cone relocation candidate with good legal residency optionality, strong civil liberties, functional infrastructure, and a favorable electricity/resource profile. Its main tradeoffs are higher regional costs, a small market, property-crime concerns in specific departments, limited direct U.S. flight connectivity, and the need for professional tax/banking review for U.S. citizens.
major_strengths: Official residency pathways include permanent and temporary routes for non-Mercosur foreigners.
Freedom House rates Uruguay Free with very high political-rights and civil-liberties scores.
Renewable electricity and high electricity access support resource resilience.
major_weaknesses: Cost of living is less favorable than lower-cost Latin American alternatives.
The U.S. State Department advises increased caution due to crime.
U.S. citizens need professional tax and banking advice before treating Uruguay as a wealth-preservation base.
open_questions: Confirm practical account-opening experience for U.S. citizens under FATCA constraints.
Verify current private health insurance pricing for older foreign residents.
Check current rental costs in Montevideo, Punta del Este, and smaller cities before assigning researched cost scores above Medium confidence.
data_gaps: Fresh city-level cost-of-living and rental data needed.
Fresh private healthcare and elder-care pricing needed.
More direct source review needed for foreign property transaction friction.

category_scores.rationale: Uruguay has official permanent and temporary residency processes, and the Ministry of Interior states that applicants who meet criteria may apply directly for permanent residency without first holding temporary residency. For Americans, the pathway is not as automatic as Mercosur residency, but it is unusually legible for the region.
strengths: Permanent residency is available to non-Mercosur foreigners.
Temporary residency can cover stays over 180 days and up to two years.
Provisional identity card rules can support limited work authorization while status is processed.
weaknesses: Document collection, apostilles, criminal background checks, and translation requirements add bureaucracy.
Citizenship/nationality treatment requires separate review before treating passport optionality as straightforward.
regional_caveats: Montevideo is the practical center for many immigration and professional-service processes.

category_scores.rationale: Uruguay has an official tax-holiday option for new tax residents covering certain foreign movable-capital income, with an election between IRNR treatment for the arrival year plus ten following fiscal years or a reduced 7% IRPF rate without time limit. This is attractive but narrow, and U.S. citizens still need U.S. tax and reporting advice.
strengths: Official DGI guidance describes favorable options for new tax residents.
Tax rules are more legible than influencer summaries suggest when official DGI guidance is used.
weaknesses: The benefit applies to specified foreign movable-capital income and does not eliminate U.S. citizen tax/reporting obligations.
Labor income, business structure, controlled companies, and treaty positions require professional advice.
